intro_html: Porkolt is the Hungarian braise most Americans call goulash, and the secret is not the meat. It is the onions. There is nearly as much onion in this pot as there is pork, cooked down until it melts into the sauce and thickens it without a speck of flour. Potatoes cook right in the pot so there is no side dish to make, and it lands at 30 grams of protein for about $3.82 (at everyday cost).
cost_closing_html: About $3.82 a bowl (at everyday cost) with the starch already in the pot. One pot, one cleanup, and dinner is handled for two weeks.
shop_smart: Buy the five pound bag of onions. This recipe uses a genuinely large amount and the bag price is far below buying them loose. Onions keep for a month in a cool dark spot.
Red bell peppers are the priciest produce line here. If the board shows them high, green peppers cost a fraction and porkolt is traditionally made with whatever pepper is around.
Good paprika is not optional in a porkolt. It is the color and the flavor. One container covers many batches, so buy a decent one and store it away from the stove heat.
Pork shoulder on sale is the whole game. It is more than half the batch cost. Buy a big one when the price drops and cut it into stew cubes yourself.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Cut the pork shoulder into stew sized cubes. Dice the onions, slice the carrots, chop the red bell peppers and cube the potatoes.
Heat the vegetable oil in a heavy pot and cook the onions slowly until they collapse and go golden. Do not rush this. The onions are your thickener and your sweetness both.
Take the pot off the heat and stir in the paprika, oregano and italian seasoning. Off heat is not a suggestion, because paprika burns in seconds and turns bitter.
Put the pot back on the burner, add the pork cubes, and stir until they lose their raw color and take on the paprika.
Add the carrots, red peppers, bay leaves, salt and black pepper, then pour in the chicken broth.
Cover and simmer low until the pork is nearly tender, stirring occasionally so nothing catches on the bottom.
Add the cubed potatoes and cook until they are soft and the sauce has thickened, then fish out the bay leaves.
portion_html: Set the full pot on your scale and subtract the empty pot weight from Step 1. Divide that total by 14 and ladle the exact amount into each container, stirring as you go so the meat and potatoes land even. Every bowl lands near 585 calories and 30 grams of protein.
